title: Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands
author: Mark Olalde
content:
A dozen Democrats in Congress are calling for limiting or banning the
construction of data centers on public lands. The moves follow [reporting from
ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org/article/burgum-public-land-data-
centers-investments) that revealed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads
the White House’s artificial intelligence push, has tens of millions of
dollars invested in AI companies.

“Our public lands aren’t a piggy bank for Trump’s powerful friends,” Sen.
Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said in [a social
media](https://x.com/SenCortezMasto/status/2119465276249116852) post that
pointed to ProPublica’s reporting. Her office told the news organization that
the senator, who serves on the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, is
working on legislation to regulate data centers on public lands and will use
the panel’s oversight authority to address concerns about transparency
surrounding them.

Burgum was asked about ProPublica’s reporting at [a recent
event](https://www.youtube.com/live/F9mHOckEmNU?si=XVNCsMJLjR-2VmpP&t=4688)
hosted by the conservative website Daily Caller. He said that his financial
reporting and ethics were “clean as a whistle,” and that he invested in
software companies before they turned to AI. “I don’t even know all the names
of the companies that are in the portfolio,” he said of his vast wealth.

[ProPublica found that hundreds of President Donald Trump’s political
appointees](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-team-financial-disclosures/)
in the executive branch, or their spouses, held stocks, owned equity or had
other financial ties to AI companies and data center developers. Other
offices, including the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Department
of Agriculture, defended their political leadership, saying the appointees
followed lawyers’ guidance and had not violated ethics rules.

Our reporting also found that [a U.S. Geological Survey
study](https://pubs.usgs.gov/sir/2026/5035/sir20265035.pdf) released earlier
this year identified an area of U.S. Department of the Interior land nearly
the size of Montana that might be suitable for data centers.

Several members of Congress pledged to float legislation to ban data center
development on this land.

“These lands are treasured and must be protected for future generations to
benefit from and enjoy,” Rep. Maxine Dexter of Oregon said in a statement. In
mid-November, [she filed the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers
Act](https://dexter.house.gov/media/press-releases/congresswoman-maxine-
dexter-md-introduces-bill-ban-data-centers-federal-public), which would ban
data center construction on land managed by the Interior Department and the
Forest Service.

Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan in July filed the [No AI Data Centers on
Federal Lands Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-
bill/9939/text), which would also prohibit their build-out on federally
managed land. The measure was dead on arrival in the Republican-controlled
House of Representatives.

“I’m going to continue building the coalition for our bill, and at the same
time, I’m going to push the Oversight Committee to investigate the outrageous
corruption of the Trump Administration,” she told ProPublica in a statement.

![A Palestinian American member of Congress holds a microphone in her right
hand while her left hand covers her heart as she speaks during an event. Out
of focus individuals are seen in the
foreground.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/GettyImages-2300554893.jpg?w=2560)Rep. Rashida Tlaib
of Michigan is one of a dozen Democratic members of Congress who have called
for limiting data center construction on public lands following recent
reporting by ProPublica. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the pushback from
Democrats in Congress.

Also speaking up were Rep. Jared Huffman of California and Sen. Martin
Heinrich of New Mexico, who serve as the ranking members of the natural
resources committees in their respective chambers. Huffman and Heinrich are in
line to take up the gavel in those committees in January when Democrats retake
the majority.

“These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to
cash in,” Heinrich said in a statement. “Public lands belong in public hands.”

Heinrich is pushing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a
generational overhaul of the legislation governing how federal agencies permit
major developments. Republicans in Congress and the White House support the
swift passage of the bill, as do some Democrats. The more environmentally
minded members of the Democratic caucus, however, are calling on Heinrich to
slow down and force a better deal once Congress reconvenes next year with
Democratic majorities.

Environmental policy experts agree that permitting reform is desperately
needed to address climate change by allowing the faster build-out of renewable
electricity generation and transmission lines. But green groups including the
Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council and League of Conservation
Voters oppose the bill because it would likely also lead to more fossil fuel
projects while limiting input on projects from Native American tribes.

The legislation presents a mixed bag for data centers. A spokesperson for
Heinrich defended the permitting reform bill, pointing out that it would
require data center companies [to bear their own
costs](https://www.whitecase.com/insight-alert/senate-permitting-bill-
bolsters-data-center-provisions-moves-full-vote) for connecting to and
upgrading the electrical grid. But the legislation would also [streamline
approval of natural gas-fired power
plants](https://time.com/article/2026/11/10/permitting-bill-data-centers/),
which power many data centers. The bill would make it more difficult to take
away a permit after it’s issued.

Meanwhile, the Interior Department [released a five-year strategic plan last
week](https://www.doi.gov/media/document/strategic-plan-fiscal-
years-2026-2030) that includes a proposal to sell off public lands or pursue
“strategic rights-of-way agreements, land exchanges and direct transfer of
lands.” It is unclear whether the department intends to offer to sell to
companies or only to local, state and tribal governments. Researchers who
study natural resources policy told ProPublica that the country’s foundational
land management law lays out steps that must be followed to dispose of federal
land, steps that will be difficult for the Trump administration to legally
navigate.

Still, with permits for data centers pending before the Interior Department,
the release of the strategic plan sparked fear that developers might try to
buy federal land. Jayson O’Neill, spokesperson for conservation group Save Our
Parks, said the plan was another attempt by Burgum to “sell off what’s left to
AI data center developers and his extractive resource buddies.”

The Interior Department did not respond to a request for comment on its
proposal to sell federal land.

The post [Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public
Lands](https://www.propublica.org/article/public-land-data-center-ban-burgum-
congress) appeared first on [ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
